reply:
Still wrong. The threat isn't limited to shell access.

If *any* process on the box gets compromised—a compromised npm package in your app, a vulnerable service, a cronjob, a dependency you didn't vet—it can write executable code to a 777 directory. This isn't theoretical. Supply chain attacks on npm, PyPI, gems, etc. are routine. The attacker doesn't need a shell; they just need code running under any user account. With 777, they can plant a backdoor script in your upload directory, nginx serves it, and you've got persistent compromise.

With 750/770 to the nginx user, a compromised dependency running in your app *as a different user* cannot write there.

The concrete cost of being wrong: A package update pulls in malicious code. It writes `shell.php` to your upload directory. Attacker has a persistent backdoor on your production box.

What would change my mind: Evidence that every process on the box runs as the nginx user and you have zero other services, no cronjobs, and no third-party code execution. That's not your setup.

Fix the ownership, not the permissions.

grade.note: Reiterates and strengthens the original stance with concrete supply-chain compromise mechanism justifying ownership+restrictive mode fix.
